annotations.annotation_text: Oneiric dimension "night" on page 385 ("Tristan and Isolde"): the nocturnal consciousness surfaces within the voyage of Tristan and Isolde observed by the Four Old Men as seagulls, Wagnerian chromatic motifs, King Mark's displacement. During this Age of Heroes (closing) phase, Joyce reconstructs the sleeping body's sensory deprivation — dimmed sight, distorted hearing, dream-logic association — transforming somatic experience into polyphonic language.
sources: Bishop, John. Joyce's Book of the Dark. https://archive.org/details/joycesbookofdark0000bish

annotations.annotation_text: Celtic/mythological figure "Ossian" on page 385 ("Tristan and Isolde"): invoking the ancient Fianna cycle and early Irish Christianity within the voyage of Tristan and Isolde observed by the Four Old Men as seagulls, Wagnerian chromatic motifs, King Mark's displacement. During the Age of Heroes (closing) phase, this mythic presence grounds the universal dream in Ireland's heroic past, linking Finn MacCool's giant body to the Dublin landscape.
sources: MacKillop, James. Dictionary of Celtic Mythology. https://www.oxfordreference.com
